provenance.summary: 8 of 189 rows carry per-row sources. The other 181 record no source: an audit on 2026-09-04 found none recorded for them anywhere, and none has been reconstructed or assumed. Sources added to rows after that audit were researched afresh and carry the date they were opened; they document the evidence as read on that date, not how the original rating was set.
provenance.sourced: Only rows that carry a "sources" field. Each entry names the page ("name"), where to open it ("url") and the date it was opened ("retrieved").
provenance.not_sourced: hazard, exposure and persistence (0-10) and evidence (1-3) are editorial ratings, not values taken from a cited dataset; "evidence" is a strength rating, not a citation. context, swap and note are editorial prose.
provenance.studies: 74 of 189 rows carry "studies": peer-reviewed or agency papers, each with a DOI and/or PMID, the score input it supports ("input": hazard, exposure or persistence), where in the paper the claim sits ("locator"), what it shows ("claim") and the date it was read ("accessed"). Every identifier was resolved on doi.org / PubMed (data/study-resolutions.json in the source repository). An input with no study is shown on its page as "unsourced input"; where a search found no fitting study, the row's "unsourced" field records the input, the search date ("searched") and the reason. The ratings themselves remain editorial.
provenance.computed: The Detox Score shown on the site is computed from hazard, exposure and persistence (100 - hazard*4.6 - exposure*3.4 - persistence*2.6, rounded, clamped 1-100) and is not stored in this file.

rows.name: Unfiltered Tap Water
rows.context: Municipal drinking water, straight from the tap
rows.swap: A filter certified to NSF/ANSI 53 or 58 for the contaminant in your water
rows.note: Quality varies widely by region. Common concerns are disinfection by-products, lead from old pipes, and trace PFAS. What a home filter removes depends on its type and on what it is certified to reduce — check the certifier’s listing for your contaminant.

studies.claim: In US EPA monitoring data from 2013-2015, drinking water supplies for 6 million US residents exceeded the 70 ng/L lifetime health advisory for PFOS and PFOA.
Pooling 6 case-control studies (2,806 cases), men averaging more than 1 µg/L of trihalomethanes had an odds ratio of 1.24 for bladder cancer, and 1.44 above 50 µg/L; no association was seen in women.
After Ronneby, Sweden, stopped supplying PFAS-contaminated municipal water, residents’ mean serum half-lives were estimated at 5.3 years for PFHxS, 3.4 years for PFOS and 2.7 years for PFOA.

sources.name: US EPA — Identifying drinking water filters certified to reduce PFAS (updated 2025-11-18)

rows.name: Bottled Water (Plastic)
rows.context: Single-use PET bottles
rows.swap: Filtered tap water in a glass or steel bottle
rows.note: Studies find microplastic and nanoplastic particles in most bottled water, shed from the plastic itself and worsened by heat and storage time.

studies.claim: 93% of 259 bottles from 11 brands showed microplastic contamination, an average of 325 particles per litre counting particles down to 6.5 um.
Micro- and nanoplastics in bottled water were estimated at about 2.4 ± 1.3 × 10^5 particles per litre.
A rapid systematic review of 3 human and 28 animal studies concluded microplastic exposure is “suspected” to harm reproductive, digestive and respiratory health; birth outcomes were “unclassifiable”.

Micro- and nanoplastics, mainly polyethylene, were found in decedents’ liver, kidney and brain; liver and brain concentrations were higher in 2024 than in 2016 deaths. A correction to the paper has been published.

rows.name: Carbon-Filter Pitcher Water
rows.context: Activated-carbon jug filter
rows.note: Pitcher filters cut many chlorination by-products, but in a 2020 home study carbon filters of this kind removed only about 40–70% of PFAS. A filter works only while its cartridge is replaced on schedule.

studies.claim: In North Carolina homes, pitcher and other activated-carbon filters (other than under-sink units) showed variable PFAS removal: about 60–70% for long-chain and about 40% for short-chain PFAS.
Filtering Barcelona tap water through a pitcher-type or reverse-osmosis filter mostly eliminated bromine-containing trihalomethanes; across all boiling and filtering tests, THM4 fell 48% to 97%.

sources.name: US EPA — Identifying drinking water filters certified to reduce PFAS (updated 2025-11-18)

rows.name: Reverse-Osmosis Filtered Water
rows.context: Under-sink RO system
rows.note: In a 2020 home study, under-sink reverse-osmosis and two-stage filters removed nearly all the PFAS tested. Like any filter, it works only while its membrane and pre-filters are replaced on schedule; RO also sends about a gallon of water to the drain for every gallon it treats.

studies.claim: In North Carolina homes, all under-sink reverse-osmosis and dual-stage filters tested showed near complete removal of all PFAS evaluated.

sources.name: US EPA — Identifying drinking water filters certified to reduce PFAS (updated 2025-11-18)

rows.name: Untested Private Well Water
rows.context: Private well, never tested
rows.swap: Annual testing + a targeted filter
rows.note: Wells aren't covered by public water rules. Arsenic, nitrates, bacteria and agricultural runoff are all possible and invisible without a test.

studies.claim: In a New England case-control study (1,213 cases), people with the highest cumulative arsenic exposure from drinking water had about twice the bladder-cancer risk of the lowest quartile (odds ratio 2.24).
About 44.1 million people in the US use domestic wells; an estimated 2.1 million (95% CI 1.5 to 2.9 million) use wells with predicted arsenic above 10 μg/L.

In a three-decade tracer experiment, 12–15% of fertilizer nitrogen still resided in soil after more than a quarter century, and nitrate export toward water is predicted to continue for at least five more decades.

rows.name: Scented Candles (Paraffin)
rows.context: Burning fragranced paraffin candles indoors
rows.swap: Unscented beeswax or soy, or none at all
rows.note: Combustion releases fine particulate and VOCs; synthetic fragrance adds more. Ventilate, or skip the flame.

studies.claim: Container candles made from different paraffin waxes, burned in a test chamber, emitted polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, aromatic compounds, short-chain aldehydes and particulate matter; wax quality strongly influenced the emissions.

rows.name: Plug-In Air Fresheners
rows.context: Continuous synthetic-fragrance diffusers
rows.swap: Open a window; simmer herbs; fix the odour source
rows.note: They mask smell by adding phthalates and VOCs to the air you breathe all day. Real ventilation beats masking every time.

studies.claim: In a 50 m3 room ventilated at about 0.5 air changes per hour, air-freshener use emitted d-limonene, dihydromyrcenol, linalool, linalyl acetate and beta-citronellol at 35-180 mg/day over 3 days.

In a 20 m3 chamber, a plug-in air freshener emitted terpenes and glycol ethers; at high ozone (about 50 ppb) its reaction products reached formaldehyde and 4-oxopentanal concentrations the authors judged may give rise to concern about sensory irritation and airflow limitation.

rows.name: Unvented Gas Stove
rows.context: Gas cooking with no range hood
rows.swap: Vent to outside; run a hood; or induction
rows.note: Gas burners emit nitrogen dioxide and fine particulate that can exceed outdoor limits in a closed kitchen. Always vent while cooking.

studies.claim: A random-effects meta-analysis of 41 studies found a summary odds ratio of 1.32 (95% CI 1.18-1.48) for asthma in children with gas cooking, and indoor NO2 associated with current wheeze (OR 1.15).

Across 87 homes in California and Colorado, gas and propane burners on high and ovens at 350 F emitted 2.8-6.5 micrograms of benzene per minute, 10-25 times more than electric coil and radiant stoves; in some homes benzene spread to bedrooms above chronic health benchmarks for hours.

rows.name: Wood-Burning Fireplace
rows.context: Open indoor wood fires
rows.swap: A sealed stove, or cleaner heating
rows.note: Wood smoke is a major source of indoor PM2.5, linked to respiratory and cardiovascular harm. If you burn, use a sealed, well-drawing stove.

studies.claim: A review concludes that wood-burning stoves and fireplaces emit significant quantities of known health-damaging pollutants, including several carcinogenic compounds, as well as CO and NOx.

rows.name: HEPA-Filtered Indoor Air
rows.context: A true-HEPA air purifier sized to the room
rows.note: One of the highest-value, lowest-effort exposure reductions: a correctly sized HEPA unit measurably cuts indoor PM2.5, pollen and many particulates.

studies.claim: In a randomized trial in 71 non-smoking homes of children with asthma, homes given two portable HEPA cleaners had 60% (95% CI 41-72%) lower sleeping-area and 42% (19-58%) lower living-area PM2.5 than control homes at one year.

rows.name: Off-Gassing New Furniture
rows.context: New pressed-wood furniture, mattresses, carpet
rows.swap: Air out new items; choose low-VOC/CertiPUR
rows.note: New composite wood and foams release formaldehyde and VOCs for weeks. Unwrap and ventilate before bringing them into bedrooms.

studies.claim: A review of 21 epidemiologic studies of indoor residential chemical emissions found formaldehyde or particleboard, phthalates or plastic materials, and recent painting to be the risk factors most often associated with respiratory or allergic effects in infants and children.

All 20 new and used crib mattresses tested in small chambers emitted VOCs, with mean total VOC emission rates of 56 micrograms/m2/h at 23 C and 139 at 36 C; rates were higher for new mattresses than used ones.

rows.name: Burning Incense
rows.context: Regular indoor incense
rows.swap: Ventilate; essential-oil diffusion sparingly
rows.note: Incense smoke can produce more fine particulate than cigarettes in a closed room. Reserve it for well-ventilated spaces.

studies.claim: In a prospective cohort of 61,320 Singapore Chinese followed to 2005, incense use was associated with a significantly increased risk of upper respiratory tract carcinomas other than nasopharyngeal, and duration and intensity of use with squamous cell carcinomas of the respiratory tract (P for trend = .004); no overall effect was seen on lung cancer.

rows.name: Secondhand Cigarette Smoke
rows.context: Living or working around indoor smoking
rows.swap: A strictly smoke-free indoor environment
rows.note: A confirmed human carcinogen with no safe level of exposure. Keeping all indoor spaces smoke-free is non-negotiable for detox load.

studies.claim: Using data from 192 countries, second-hand smoke was estimated to have caused 603,000 deaths in 2004, about 1.0% of worldwide mortality, including 379,000 from ischaemic heart disease and 21,400 from lung cancer.

rows.name: Nonstick (PTFE) Cookware
rows.context: Teflon-type nonstick pans
rows.swap: Cast iron or stainless steel
rows.note: Scratched or overheated nonstick can shed PFAS-family compounds — the 'forever chemicals' that persist in the body and environment for years.

studies.claim: Four brands of nonstick frying pans released 7-337 ng of PFOA per pan into the gas phase at normal cooking surface temperatures (179-233 °C).

rows.name: Cast Iron Cookware
rows.context: Seasoned cast-iron pans
rows.note: No synthetic coating to break down. A well-seasoned pan is naturally nonstick and can even add dietary iron.

rows.name: Stainless Steel Cookware
rows.context: 18/10 stainless pans and pots
rows.note: Inert, durable, coating-free. The safe default for everyday high-heat cooking.

rows.name: Uncoated Aluminum Cookware
rows.context: Bare aluminum pots and foil with acidic food
rows.swap: Anodized aluminum or stainless steel
rows.note: Bare aluminum can leach into acidic foods like tomato sauce. Anodized or stainless removes the concern.

rows.name: Plastic Cutting Boards
rows.context: Cutting on soft plastic boards
rows.swap: Wood or bamboo boards
rows.note: Knife scoring sheds microplastic particles directly into your food. Wood is naturally antimicrobial and doesn't shed.

rows.name: Conventional Strawberries
rows.context: Non-organic strawberries (a 'Dirty Dozen' crop)
rows.swap: Organic strawberries, or peel-heavy fruit instead
rows.note: Consistently among the most pesticide-laden produce. This is a crop where buying organic meaningfully cuts residue.

studies.claim: In 3 years of field trials, all active ingredients except propargite fell below EU maximum residue levels in ripe strawberries, but most of the fungicides tested often persisted above 0.01 mg/kg, the baby-food limit.

rows.name: Organic Strawberries
rows.context: Certified-organic strawberries
rows.note: Grown without synthetic pesticides. For high-residue crops, the organic version is a genuine exposure reduction.

studies.claim: A meta-analysis of 343 peer-reviewed publications found pesticide residues four times more frequent in conventional crops than in organic ones, which also had lower cadmium.

rows.name: Conventional Spinach
rows.context: Non-organic leafy greens
rows.swap: Organic greens; wash thoroughly
rows.note: Leafy greens carry high pesticide residue because you eat the whole leaf. A strong candidate for buying organic.

rows.name: Canned Food (BPA Lining)
rows.context: Canned goods with epoxy linings
rows.swap: Glass jars, cartons, or 'BPA-free' cans
rows.note: BPA and its substitutes migrate from can linings into food, especially acidic and fatty contents. Choose glass or verified BPA-free packaging.

studies.claim: In 7,669 NHANES 2003-2008 participants, one canned food in the past 24 hours went with 24% higher urinary BPA and two or more with 54%; canned soup with 229%.

EFSA's panel set a tolerable daily intake for BPA of 0.2 ng/kg body weight, with the immune system as the most sensitive target, and found average and high dietary exposures in all age groups exceeded it by two to three orders of magnitude.

rows.name: Large Predatory Fish
rows.context: Tuna, swordfish, king mackerel, shark
rows.swap: Small fish: sardines, anchovies, wild salmon
rows.note: Mercury bioaccumulates up the food chain, concentrating in big long-lived predators. Small oily fish give the omega-3s with far less mercury.

studies.claim: Ranking 51 seafood varieties by their share of mercury in the US seafood supply, tuna (canned and fresh) accounted for 37.4% of total mercury inputs, while most of the highest-mercury fish except swordfish were minor contributors.

In a Faroe Islands birth cohort of 1,022 children, prenatal methylmercury exposure from the mother's diet was linked at age 7 to poorer language, attention and memory, still seen after excluding children whose mothers had hair mercury above 10 µg/g.

In 27 volunteers who ate fish at the tolerable weekly methylmercury intake for 14 weeks, blood mercury rose from 6.7 to 26.9 ng/g, and its half-life after they stopped was 94 days (57 days after subtracting background).

rows.name: Small Oily Fish (Sardines)
rows.context: Sardines, anchovies, herring
rows.note: Low on the food chain means low mercury, plus excellent omega-3s that support overall metabolic health.

rows.name: Cruciferous Vegetables
rows.context: Broccoli, cauliflower, cabbage, Brussels sprouts
rows.note: Contain sulforaphane, which upregulates the body's own phase-II detoxification enzymes. One of the few foods that actively supports your detox systems.

rows.name: Ultra-Processed Food
rows.context: Packaged snacks, sodas, ready meals
rows.swap: Whole, minimally processed foods
rows.note: Carries additives, emulsifiers, and packaging-derived compounds, and displaces the fiber and phytonutrients your detox pathways rely on.

studies.claim: Among 2,212 NHANES 2013-2014 participants, each 10% more energy from ultra-processed food went with 8.0% higher urinary MCOP, a phthalate metabolite, with a stronger association in children; bisphenols were not associated.

rows.name: Charred Grilled Meat
rows.context: Blackened, flame-grilled red meat
rows.swap: Lower-temp cooking; trim char; marinate
rows.note: High-heat charring forms heterocyclic amines and PAHs. Marinating, avoiding flare-ups and scraping off char cuts their formation.

studies.claim: In gas-grilled beef grilled at 150-350 °C, PAHs and heterocyclic amines both rose with temperature; benzo[a]pyrene was in every sample, and PAH4 at 300 and 350 °C exceeded the EU maximum level. Marinating cut most heterocyclic amines.

rows.name: White Rice (Arsenic)
rows.context: Rice, especially for daily eaters and infants
rows.swap: Rinse well, cook in excess water; vary grains
rows.note: Rice takes up inorganic arsenic from soil and water. Rinsing and cooking in a high water-to-rice ratio removes a meaningful share.

studies.claim: Parboiling rice in fresh water and then cooking it by absorption removed 73% of the inorganic arsenic from white rice and 54% from brown rice.

EFSA's contaminants panel found chronic dietary inorganic arsenic linked to cancers of the skin, bladder and lung, treated it as a genotoxic carcinogen, and judged that adult exposure margins (2 to 0.4 for average consumers) raise a health concern.

rows.name: Filtered Black Coffee
rows.context: Paper-filtered coffee
rows.note: Paper filtering removes cafestol; the drink itself is rich in antioxidants. A low-burden daily habit for most people.

rows.name: Synthetic Fragrance / Perfume
rows.context: 'Parfum' in perfume, lotion, and sprays
rows.swap: Fragrance-free, or essential-oil scented sparingly
rows.note: 'Fragrance' is an undisclosed mixture that often includes phthalates used to make scent linger. Fragrance-free is the simplest cut.

rows.name: Aluminum Antiperspirant
rows.context: Daily aluminum-based antiperspirant
rows.swap: Aluminum-free deodorant if you prefer
rows.note: Evidence of harm is weak and contested, but it's an easy swap for anyone who wants to reduce daily aluminum contact on skin.

rows.name: Conventional Shampoo
rows.context: Shampoo with parabens and harsh surfactants
rows.swap: Paraben-free, simpler formulas
rows.note: Leave-on and rinse-off products add up across the day. Simpler, paraben- and fragrance-free formulas reduce the cumulative load.

rows.name: Nail Salon Products
rows.context: Gel/acrylic nails, frequent salon visits
rows.swap: '3-free/9-free' polish; ventilated salons
rows.note: The 'toxic trio' — toluene, formaldehyde, DBP — plus solvent fumes make salons a real inhalation exposure. Choose ventilated shops and cleaner polishes.

rows.name: Oxybenzone Sunscreen
rows.context: Chemical sunscreens with oxybenzone
rows.swap: Mineral (zinc oxide) sunscreen
rows.note: Oxybenzone absorbs through skin and is an environmental concern. Mineral sunscreens protect just as well without it — and sunscreen itself stays essential.

rows.name: Fragrance-Free Basic Skincare
rows.context: Simple, unscented moisturizer and cleanser
rows.note: Fewer ingredients means fewer unknowns. A short, fragrance-free routine is the low-burden default for skin.

rows.name: Conventional All-Purpose Cleaner
rows.context: Fragranced spray cleaners with QUATs/VOCs
rows.swap: Simple vinegar/soap solutions; fragrance-free
rows.note: Sprays aerosolize cleaning chemicals right into your breathing zone. Fragrance-free or DIY basics handle most household jobs.

rows.name: Frequent Unventilated Bleach
rows.context: Regular bleach use in closed rooms
rows.swap: Ventilate; use only when needed; never mix
rows.note: Bleach fumes irritate airways and form dangerous gases if mixed with ammonia or acids. Reserve it for real disinfection and open windows.

rows.name: Dryer Sheets & Fabric Softener
rows.context: Scented laundry softeners and sheets
rows.swap: Wool dryer balls; skip softener
rows.note: Coat fabric — and skin — in fragrance and quaternary compounds, then vent scented VOCs outdoors. Wool dryer balls do the softening job cleanly.

studies.claim: More than 25 VOCs were emitted from dryer vents during use of fragranced laundry products, seven of them hazardous air pollutants and two carcinogenic (acetaldehyde, benzene).

rows.name: Vinegar & Baking Soda Cleaning
rows.context: DIY cleaning basics: vinegar and baking soda
rows.note: Handles the majority of everyday cleaning with near-zero inhalation or residue burden. The low-cost, low-exposure baseline.

rows.name: Home & Garden Pesticide Sprays
rows.context: DIY insecticides and weed killers
rows.swap: Physical controls; targeted, minimal use
rows.note: Consumer pesticides drift indoors and settle into dust. Prefer traps, barriers and spot-treatment over broadcast spraying.

rows.name: Stain-Resistant Textiles (PFAS)
rows.context: 'Stain-proof' carpets, sofas, jackets
rows.swap: Untreated fabrics; skip the stain-guard add-on
rows.note: Stain and water repellency usually means PFAS coatings that shed into dust and never break down. Decline the optional stain treatment.

studies.claim: In 178 women, having stain-resistant carpet or furniture was associated with higher levels of some serum PFASs.

Multiple studies link PFAS exposure to adverse immune outcomes in children, and dyslipidemia is the strongest metabolic outcome; cancer evidence is limited to manufacturing locations with extremely high exposures.
After residents of Ronneby, Sweden, stopped drinking PFAS-contaminated water, their mean serum half-lives were estimated at 5.3 years for PFHxS, 3.4 years for PFOS and 2.7 years for PFOA.

rows.name: Vinyl (PVC) Shower Curtain
rows.context: That 'new shower curtain' smell
rows.swap: Fabric (polyester/cotton) or EVA curtain
rows.note: The smell is phthalates off-gassing in a warm, humid room you breathe in daily. Fabric curtains wash and last without it.

rows.name: Settled House Dust
rows.context: Accumulated dust on floors and surfaces
rows.swap: HEPA vacuum + damp dusting; doormats
rows.note: House dust concentrates flame retardants, PFAS and phthalates — a bigger everyday exposure route than most people realize. Regular HEPA vacuuming genuinely lowers it.

studies.claim: A meta-analysis of US indoor dust found phthalates, phenols, replacement flame retardants, fragrances and PFASs consistently present; several phthalates and flame retardants had the highest residential intakes.

rows.name: Heating Food in Plastic
rows.context: Microwaving or storing hot food in plastic
rows.swap: Glass or ceramic for anything warm
rows.note: Heat dramatically increases how much plastic and its additives migrate into food. Never microwave in plastic; transfer hot food to glass.

rows.name: Plastic Wrap on Hot Food
rows.context: Cling film touching warm, fatty food
rows.swap: Let food cool; use a plate or beeswax wrap
rows.note: Plasticizers migrate readily into hot, fatty foods. Cool food before covering, or use a lid instead of film.

rows.name: Glass Food Storage
rows.context: Glass containers for leftovers and meal prep
rows.note: Inert, heat-safe and non-shedding. The single best swap to remove plastic-to-food migration from your kitchen.

rows.name: Thermal Paper Receipts
rows.context: Handling glossy receipts, especially with lotion
rows.swap: Decline receipts; go digital; wash hands
rows.note: The coating is often BPA/BPS, absorbed through skin — more so with hand sanitizer or lotion on. Skip the paper receipt when you can.

studies.claim: Holding thermal receipt paper right after using a hand sanitizer transferred BPA to hands and food, raising unconjugated serum BPA to an average peak of about 7 ng/mL within 90 minutes.

rows.name: Hot Greasy Takeout Containers
rows.context: Molded-fiber bowls and grease-proof wrappers
rows.swap: Transfer food out; cook at home more often
rows.note: Grease-resistant food packaging is a known PFAS source, and hot food speeds migration. Move takeout onto a plate promptly.

studies.claim: Of 42 Canadian fast-food packaging samples, molded “compostable” bowls had the highest total fluorine (1,010,000-1,300,000 µg F/m²); the high-fluorine samples each held 4-15 individual PFAS.
US FDA migration tests found mg/kg amounts of perfluoro paper additives and coatings transferring to food oil.

Multiple studies link PFAS exposure to adverse immune outcomes in children, and dyslipidemia is the strongest metabolic outcome; cancer evidence is limited to manufacturing locations with extremely high exposures.

unsourced.reason: The PFAS measured here are mainly short-chain or fluorotelomer compounds; the human half-life studies found cover long-chain PFAS (PFOS, PFOA, PFHxS), so none is cited.

rows.name: Canned & Reused Plastic Bottles
rows.context: Refilling single-use bottles; canned drinks
rows.swap: A dedicated steel or glass reusable
rows.note: Single-use bottles aren't built for reuse — wear and heat increase leaching and bacterial growth. A proper reusable is cleaner and cheaper over time.

rows.name: Roadside & Traffic Air
rows.context: Living, running, or cycling next to heavy traffic
rows.swap: Exercise away from traffic; filter home air
rows.note: Traffic exhaust delivers PM2.5, benzene and ultrafine particles. Move workouts to parks and back streets, and filter indoor air near busy roads.

rows.name: Regular Sauna Use
rows.context: Consistent sauna or heat bathing
rows.note: Associated with cardiovascular benefits and supports the body's natural processes through heat adaptation and sweating. Hydrate well and listen to your body.

rows.name: New-Car Interior Off-Gassing
rows.context: That 'new car smell'
rows.swap: Ventilate; park in shade; air it out for weeks
rows.note: The smell is VOCs and flame retardants off-gassing from plastics and adhesives, worse in heat. Ventilate generously for the first months.

rows.name: Dry-Cleaned Clothes (Perc)
rows.context: Traditional perchloroethylene dry cleaning
rows.swap: Air out garments; choose 'green' cleaners
rows.note: Perc is a probable carcinogen that lingers in freshly cleaned fabric. Air garments outside the bag before wearing, or use wet/green cleaners.

studies.claim: Polyester, cotton and wool retained micromolar levels of PCE that rose over successive dry-cleaning cycles and volatilised slowly in room air; silk retained little.

rows.name: Untested Basement Radon
rows.context: Lower-floor living space, never tested for radon
rows.swap: A cheap radon test kit, then mitigate if high
rows.note: Radon is the second-leading cause of lung cancer and is completely invisible. A one-time test is among the highest-value things on this whole list.

rows.name: Regular Exercise & Sweat
rows.context: Consistent physical activity
rows.note: Supports circulation, lymphatic flow and overall metabolic health — the foundation your body's own clearance systems run on. Not a 'detox' shortcut, but the real thing.

rows.name: Microwave Popcorn Bags
rows.context: The grease-proof lining of microwave popcorn bags
rows.swap: Air-pop plain kernels in a pot or a plain paper bag
rows.note: The non-stick lining has historically used PFAS 'forever chemicals' that can migrate into the oil and popcorn when heated. Loose kernels cost less and skip the coating entirely.

studies.claim: 5-34 ng of PFOA was found in the vapours produced from a prepacked microwave popcorn bag.
In NHANES 2003-2014, eating popcorn was associated with significantly higher serum PFOA, PFNA, PFDA and PFOS.

rows.name: Plastic Tea Bags
rows.context: Pyramid-style mesh tea bags steeped in boiling water
rows.swap: Loose-leaf tea with a stainless-steel infuser, or unbleached paper bags
rows.note: Nylon and PET mesh bags can shed microplastics into hot water. Loose leaf or paper bags avoid the plastic and often taste better.

studies.claim: Steeping one nylon or PET plastic teabag at 95 °C released about 11.6 billion microplastic and 3.1 billion nanoplastic particles into a single cup.

rows.name: Dark Chocolate (Heavy Metals)
rows.context: Cocoa-heavy dark chocolate eaten regularly
rows.swap: Enjoy in moderation and favour brands that publish third-party heavy-metal testing
rows.note: Cocoa can carry trace cadmium and lead from soil and processing. Occasional squares are fine; the concern is large daily amounts, especially for children.

studies.claim: Of 72 US cocoa products tested between 2014 and 2022, 43% exceeded California's Prop 65 daily maximum for lead and 35% for cadmium per serving; organic products were more likely to carry higher lead and cadmium.

rows.name: Farmed Salmon
rows.context: Conventionally farmed Atlantic salmon
rows.swap: Wild-caught salmon, or smaller oily fish like sardines and mackerel
rows.note: Farmed fish can carry more of certain fat-soluble contaminants than wild. It is still a good protein source — variety and smaller species lower the load.

studies.claim: Analysing over 2 metric tons of farmed and wild salmon from around the world, organochlorine contaminant concentrations were significantly higher in farmed than in wild salmon, and highest in European-farmed fish.

rows.name: Mothballs (Naphthalene)
rows.context: Naphthalene or paradichlorobenzene mothballs in closets
rows.swap: Cedar blocks, lavender sachets, or sealed garment bags
rows.note: Mothballs slowly sublimate into a gas you breathe in enclosed spaces. Physical barriers and natural deterrents protect clothes without the fumes.

rows.name: Vinyl (PVC) Flooring
rows.context: Flexible vinyl plank or sheet flooring
rows.swap: Sealed hardwood, tile, or verified phthalate-free flooring
rows.note: Soft PVC flooring can off-gas phthalate plasticisers, especially when new and warm. Hard, inert surfaces avoid the issue.

studies.claim: Infants with PVC flooring in the bedroom had significantly higher urinary levels of MBzP, a metabolite of the phthalate BBzP (83 urine samples).

rows.name: Antibacterial Soap (Triclosan)
rows.context: Hand and body washes marketed as antibacterial
rows.swap: Plain soap and water — equally effective for everyday handwashing
rows.note: Triclosan is a persistent antimicrobial with no proven benefit over plain soap for home use, and it ends up in waterways. Regulators have already pulled it from many products.

rows.name: Talc-Based Body Powder
rows.context: Loose talcum powder used on skin
rows.swap: Cornstarch-based powder
rows.note: The concern is possible asbestos contamination in mined talc and inhalation of fine particles. Cornstarch powders sidestep both.

rows.name: Permanent Hair Dye
rows.context: Oxidative permanent hair colour applied at home or salon
rows.swap: Henna, semi-permanent dyes, or less frequent application in a ventilated space
rows.note: Permanent dyes contain aromatic amines absorbed through the scalp. Spacing out applications and good ventilation reduce the dose.

rows.name: Old Lead Paint
rows.context: Deteriorating paint in homes built before the late 1970s
rows.swap: Professional lead-safe remediation — never dry-sand it yourself
rows.note: Lead paint dust is one of the most serious avoidable household exposures, especially for young children. Disturbing it wrong makes it far worse; use certified remediation.

rows.name: Plastic Children's Toys
rows.context: Soft plastic toys, especially older or imported ones
rows.swap: Wood, silicone, or certified phthalate-free toys
rows.note: Soft plastics can contain phthalates that children mouth and handle. Modern certified toys limit these; the risk is mostly older or unregulated imports.

rows.name: Chlorinated Shower Water
rows.context: Hot showers in chlorinated municipal water
rows.swap: Shorter showers
rows.note: Hot showers release chloroform and other disinfection by-products into the air you breathe, and some are absorbed through the skin. In a volunteer study, one of them, bromodichloromethane, fell to near undetectable blood levels within a day of skin exposure.

studies.claim: In a New England case-control study, the highest showering/bathing category for brominated trihalomethanes gave a bladder-cancer odds ratio of 1.43 (95% CI 0.80–2.42); the authors concluded a modest association for ingestion.
In 100 volunteers taking controlled 10-minute showers, geometric mean total trihalomethanes in air rose from 5.8 to 351 μg/m3, and in blood from 16.5 to 299 ng/L.
In a controlled study of six people, 56% of chloroform was released from shower water to air, and inhalation during a typical 10–15 minute shower contributed significantly to total chloroform dose.
After a 1-hour forearm soak in water containing bromodichloromethane, blood levels fell to near or below detection by 24 hours; after drinking, levels returned near or below detection within 4 hours.

rows.name: Black Plastic Kitchen Utensils
rows.context: Black nylon/plastic spatulas and serving spoons
rows.swap: Stainless steel or solid wood utensils
rows.note: Some black plastic kitchenware is made from recycled electronic plastic and can carry brominated flame retardants that migrate into hot food. Metal or wood avoids the issue.

rows.name: Nonstick Air Fryer Basket
rows.context: PTFE-coated air fryer baskets and trays
rows.swap: A stainless-steel or ceramic-coated basket
rows.note: High-heat cooking on scratched PTFE coatings can release fumes and shed particles. Uncoated stainless or a ceramic liner sidesteps the fluorinated coating.

rows.name: Melamine Dishware
rows.context: Melamine plates and bowls used with hot food
rows.swap: Glass, ceramic or stainless dishware
rows.note: Melamine can migrate from the dish into hot, acidic or microwaved food. It is fine for cold use, but keep it away from heat, or switch to glass.

rows.name: Silicone Bakeware
rows.context: Food-grade silicone moulds and mats
rows.note: Good-quality food-grade silicone is stable and low-migration at normal baking temperatures. Choose platinum-cured silicone and avoid cheap fillers for the cleanest option.

rows.name: Conventional Apples
rows.context: Non-organic apples eaten with skin
rows.swap: Organic apples, or wash and peel
rows.note: Apples rank high on pesticide-residue testing because residues concentrate in the skin. Washing helps, peeling helps more, and organic avoids most of it.

studies.claim: Residues of five pesticides were higher in apple peel and core than in the flesh; washing removed 6.7-67% depending on the compound, and peeling and coring significantly reduced residues in the edible part for all but beta-cypermethrin.

rows.name: Conventional Grapes
rows.context: Non-organic table grapes
rows.swap: Organic grapes, or a thorough rinse
rows.note: Grapes routinely show multiple pesticide residues on residue-monitoring lists. A good rinse cuts surface residue; organic avoids most of it.

studies.claim: Of 280 table-grape samples bought in Turkey in 2016, 59.6% carried one or more pesticide residues and 20.4% exceeded EU maximum residue levels; the worst-case hazard index was 3.37% for adults and 9.42% for children.

rows.name: Deli Meats
rows.context: Processed sliced ham, salami and cured meats
rows.swap: Fresh-roasted meat you slice yourself
rows.note: Processed meats are classified as a group 1 carcinogen, driven partly by nitrite-formed nitrosamines. Occasional use is one thing; daily deli sandwiches add up.

studies.claim: Pooling 29 prospective cohort studies, high versus low processed-meat intake gave a relative risk of 1.13 for colorectal cancer and 1.19 for colon cancer; the authors judge most included studies at serious risk of bias and urge cautious interpretation.

rows.name: Canned Tuna
rows.context: Albacore/white canned tuna eaten frequently
rows.swap: Light skipjack tuna or small oily fish like sardines
rows.note: Larger tuna accumulate methylmercury, which builds up in the body. Choosing smaller 'light' tuna or sardines keeps the omega-3s with far less mercury.

studies.claim: In 168 cans bought in New Jersey from 1998 to 2003, white (albacore) tuna averaged 0.407 ppm mercury against 0.118 ppm for light tuna, and 25% of white tuna cans exceeded 0.5 ppm.

In a Faroe Islands birth cohort of 1,022 children, prenatal methylmercury exposure from the mother's diet was linked at age 7 to poorer language, attention and memory, still seen after excluding children whose mothers had hair mercury above 10 µg/g.

In 27 volunteers who ate fish at the tolerable weekly methylmercury intake for 14 weeks, blood mercury rose from 6.7 to 26.9 ng/g, and its half-life after they stopped was 94 days (57 days after subtracting background).

rows.name: Protein Powder
rows.context: Daily protein-powder shakes
rows.swap: A third-party heavy-metal-tested powder, or whole-food protein
rows.note: Independent testing has found lead, cadmium and arsenic in some protein powders, especially plant and chocolate varieties. Look for published heavy-metal testing.

rows.name: Conventional Makeup (PFAS)
rows.context: Long-wear foundation, mascara and lipstick
rows.swap: Cosmetics labelled PFAS-free
rows.note: Studies have detected PFAS 'forever chemicals' in many long-wear and waterproof cosmetics, applied daily right on the skin. PFAS-free lines avoid them.

studies.claim: Of 231 US and Canadian cosmetics screened, foundations, mascaras and lip products most often had elevated fluorine; 29 analysed products held PFAS at 22-10,500 ng/g, mostly undisclosed on the label.

Multiple studies link PFAS exposure to adverse immune outcomes in children, and dyslipidemia is the strongest metabolic outcome; cancer evidence is limited to manufacturing locations with extremely high exposures.

unsourced.reason: The PFAS measured here are mainly short-chain or fluorotelomer compounds; the human half-life studies found cover long-chain PFAS (PFOS, PFOA, PFHxS), so none is cited.

rows.name: Scented Body Wash
rows.context: Fragranced shower gels and washes
rows.swap: A fragrance-free or essential-oil-only wash
rows.note: 'Fragrance' can hide phthalates used to make scent last. You rinse it off, but daily whole-body use adds up — fragrance-free removes the guesswork.

rows.name: Chemical Hair Relaxers
rows.context: Chemical straightening and relaxer treatments
rows.swap: Skip chemical straightening; heat-style sparingly
rows.note: Large studies link frequent chemical hair-straightener use to hormone-related health risks, and some release formaldehyde. Reducing frequency lowers the exposure.

rows.name: Conventional Body Lotion
rows.context: Fragranced lotions with parabens
rows.swap: A fragrance-free, paraben-free lotion
rows.note: Applied over a large skin area daily, paraben-and-fragrance lotions are a steady low-level exposure. Simple fragrance-free formulas do the same job.

rows.name: PFAS-Coated Dental Floss
rows.context: Slick PTFE/PFAS-coated 'glide' floss
rows.swap: Uncoated or natural-wax floss
rows.note: Some smooth 'glide' flosses are PTFE-based, and research has associated their use with higher PFAS levels. Plain waxed floss works just as well.

studies.claim: In 178 women, flossing with Oral-B Glide was associated with higher levels of some serum PFASs; Glide and competitor flosses tested positive for fluorine.

rows.name: Flame-Retardant Furniture Foam
rows.context: Older upholstered sofas and chairs with FR foam
rows.swap: Furniture labelled free of added flame retardants (TB117-2013)
rows.note: Older upholstered foam often contains persistent flame retardants that migrate into house dust. Newer 'no added flame retardants' labelling avoids them.

rows.name: Conventional Mattress
rows.context: New synthetic mattress off-gassing
rows.swap: A CertiPUR-US or GOTS/GOLS-certified mattress; air out new ones
rows.note: You spend a third of your life in contact with it, and new synthetic mattresses can off-gas VOCs and carry flame retardants. Certified low-emission foam or natural latex reduces both.

rows.name: New Carpet
rows.context: Freshly installed wall-to-wall carpet
rows.swap: Low-VOC hard flooring or untreated wool rugs
rows.note: New carpet can off-gas VOCs and often carries PFAS-based stain treatment that ends up in house dust. Hard flooring or untreated natural fibres avoids the stain chemistry.

studies.claim: In NHANES 2005-2006, people in homes with low pile carpet had significantly higher serum PFHxS and MeFOSAA than those with smooth floors; about 24% and 19% of those body burdens were attributed to carpeting. The study did not separate new from old carpet.

rows.name: Antibacterial Wipes
rows.context: Quat-based disinfecting wipes used daily
rows.swap: Plain soap and water, or plant-based cleaners
rows.note: Quaternary ammonium 'quat' disinfectants are respiratory irritants and are overkill for everyday surfaces. Soap and water handles most home cleaning.

rows.name: Pressed-Wood Furniture
rows.context: Particleboard and MDF furniture off-gassing
rows.swap: Solid wood or CARB2 / formaldehyde-free rated pieces
rows.note: Particleboard and MDF glues can off-gas formaldehyde, a known irritant and carcinogen, for months. Solid wood or low-emission certified board reduces it.

rows.name: Polyester Clothing
rows.context: Synthetic fabrics that shed microfibres
rows.swap: Natural fibres — cotton, wool, linen; a microfibre laundry bag
rows.note: Synthetic clothing sheds plastic microfibres in the wash and through wear, adding to microplastic exposure. Natural fibres and a filter bag cut the shedding.

studies.claim: Real-scale household washes released 124-308 mg of microfibres per kg of synthetic garments, i.e. 640,000 to 1,500,000 microfibres.

rows.name: Disposable Coffee Cups
rows.context: Plastic-lined paper cups for hot drinks
rows.swap: A reusable ceramic or stainless cup
rows.note: The thin plastic lining that makes paper cups waterproof can shed microplastic particles into hot liquid. A reusable cup avoids the daily dose.

rows.name: Vinyl (PVC) Yoga Mat
rows.context: Soft PVC exercise and yoga mats
rows.swap: A TPE, cork or natural-rubber mat
rows.note: Flexible PVC mats can contain phthalate plasticisers and give off that 'new plastic' smell. TPE, cork or rubber mats skip the PVC chemistry.

rows.name: Old Lead Plumbing
rows.context: Lead service lines or old solder in home plumbing
rows.swap: Test the water, use a filter certified to NSF/ANSI 53 for lead, and replace the lead line
rows.note: Lead pipes and solder can leach lead into tap water, and harm has been measured even at low blood-lead levels. Have the water tested, and use a filter certified to NSF/ANSI 53 for lead until the line is replaced.

studies.claim: In 14,289 US adults followed for a median 19.3 years, a rise in blood lead from 1.0 to 6.7 μg/dL was associated with all-cause mortality (hazard ratio 1.37) and cardiovascular mortality (1.70).
Pooling 1,333 children from seven cohorts, a rise in blood lead from 2.4 to 10 μg/dL was associated with a 3.9-point IQ decrement (95% CI 2.4–5.3).
Among 63,854 Washington DC children, lead service lines were an independent risk factor for blood lead of 10 and 5 μg/dL or more, even when the water met the EPA 15 ppb action level.

Across census tracts served by the Cincinnati and Grand Rapids water systems, lead service line prevalence correlated strongly with children’s elevated blood lead (5 μg/dL or more): r = 0.71 and r = 0.83.

After occupational exposure, blood lead declines slowly, with a 5- to 19-year half-life reflecting lead’s long stay in the skeleton; repeated bone measurements show slow elimination of lead from bone.

rows.name: Chlorinated Pool Water
rows.context: Frequent indoor chlorinated-pool swimming
rows.swap: Rinse before and after; well-ventilated or saltwater pools
rows.note: Chlorine reacts with sweat and skin oils to form disinfection by-products you absorb and inhale, worst in poorly ventilated indoor pools. Showering first and good ventilation help.

rows.name: Wildfire Smoke
rows.context: Fine-particle smoke during wildfire season
rows.swap: HEPA air purifier indoors; a fitted N95 outdoors
rows.note: Wildfire smoke is loaded with fine PM2.5 that reaches deep into the lungs. On smoky days, a HEPA purifier indoors and a fitted N95 outdoors cut what you breathe in.

rows.name: Aluminum Foil (Cooking)
rows.context: Wrapping or cooking hot, acidic food in foil
rows.swap: Parchment paper, or cook in a glass or ceramic dish
rows.note: Small amounts of aluminum migrate into food, more so with heat and acidic ingredients like tomato or lemon. Everyday amounts are generally considered low-risk, but you can avoid the transfer entirely with an inert surface.

rows.name: Plastic Coffee Pods (K-Cups)
rows.context: Single-serve plastic pods brewed with near-boiling water
rows.swap: A reusable stainless-steel pod, or a French press or moka pot
rows.note: Forcing hot water through a thin plastic pod can release microplastics and, from some plastics, trace additives. A steel filter avoids the disposable plastic entirely.

rows.name: Fabric Protector Spray (PFAS)
rows.context: Aftermarket stain-repellent sprays for furniture, shoes and carpet
rows.swap: Skip the spray; choose untreated natural-fibre textiles and blot spills promptly
rows.note: Many stain and water repellents rely on PFAS, the persistent fluorinated compounds that build up in the body and environment. Aerosol application also means you inhale the mist.

studies.claim: Spraying a fluorinated-polymer stain-repellent resin gave significant near-field exposure to overspray mist; the authors relate the sprayers' acute respiratory illness to the fluorinated polymer itself.

rows.name: Glyphosate Weed Killer
rows.context: Home garden and lawn herbicide use
rows.swap: Manual weeding, mulching, or a vinegar-based spot herbicide
rows.note: Glyphosate residues are widely detected and its hazard classification is debated by regulators. For home use, non-chemical weed control removes the exposure and the drift onto edible plants.

rows.name: DEET Insect Repellent
rows.context: Skin-applied mosquito and tick repellent
rows.swap: Apply to clothing rather than skin, or use a picaridin repellent
rows.note: DEET is registered and effective at preventing insect-borne disease, and that protection often outweighs the exposure. To reduce contact, use the lowest effective concentration and wash it off once indoors.

rows.name: Conventional Kale
rows.context: Non-organic kale, a frequent pesticide-residue crop
rows.swap: Organic kale, or wash and soak thoroughly before eating
rows.note: Leafy greens like kale regularly appear high on pesticide-residue rankings. The vegetable itself is nutritious — the exposure is the residue, which washing and organic sourcing reduce.

rows.name: Conventional Peaches
rows.context: Non-organic peaches and nectarines
rows.swap: Organic peaches, or peel and wash conventional ones
rows.note: Soft-skinned stone fruit tends to carry more surface pesticide residue. Choosing organic or peeling reduces the residue you consume without giving up the fruit.

rows.name: Microwave Frozen Meals (Plastic Tray)
rows.context: Heating a ready meal in its plastic tray or film
rows.swap: Transfer the food to a glass or ceramic dish before microwaving
rows.note: Microwaving in plastic is one of the biggest drivers of chemical and microplastic migration into food, because heat accelerates the transfer. Moving the food to glass first avoids it.

rows.name: Fast-Food Wrappers (PFAS)
rows.context: Grease-resistant wrappers, bags and boxes for hot food
rows.swap: Unwrap greasy food promptly, or cook the same meals at home
rows.note: Grease-proof food packaging has often been treated with PFAS, which can migrate into hot, oily food. Getting the food out of the wrapper quickly limits the contact time.

studies.claim: Of about 400 US fast-food packaging samples, 46% of food-contact papers and 20% of paperboard samples had detectable fluorine.

rows.name: Turmeric Supplements (Lead)
rows.context: Bulk or imported turmeric powder and capsules
rows.swap: Buy turmeric from brands that publish heavy-metal testing
rows.note: Some turmeric has been adulterated with lead-based colourant to brighten it, a documented source of lead exposure. Third-party-tested brands avoid the problem.

studies.claim: Across Bangladesh's turmeric supply chain, lead chromate pigment adulteration was found in 7 of the 9 major producing districts, with turmeric powder reaching 1,152 µg/g lead.

rows.name: Ground Cinnamon (Lead)
rows.context: Some imported ground cinnamon and cinnamon products
rows.swap: Use Ceylon cinnamon from tested, reputable brands
rows.note: Recent recalls found elevated lead in certain cinnamon and cinnamon-flavoured products. The spice in normal amounts is fine — the concern is contamination in specific low-quality supply chains.

studies.claim: After FDA traced lead and chromium to the cinnamon in recalled applesauce pouches, 566 US cases with blood lead of at least 3.5 µg/dL were reported between November 2023 and April 2024, 55% in children under 2.

rows.name: Aerosol Dry Shampoo (Benzene)
rows.context: Spray-can dry shampoo used near the scalp
rows.swap: A non-aerosol powder dry shampoo, or simply washing your hair
rows.note: Testing has found benzene, a known carcinogen, contaminating some aerosol dry shampoos from the propellant. Powder formats avoid both the contaminant and the inhaled mist.

rows.name: Aerosol Sunscreen Spray (Benzene)
rows.context: Spray sunscreens found to contain benzene contamination
rows.swap: A mineral (zinc oxide) lotion sunscreen
rows.note: Several spray sunscreens were recalled after benzene was detected. Sun protection still matters — a lotion, especially a mineral one, gives the protection without the propellant and contamination risk.

rows.name: Conventional Tampons
rows.context: Scented or conventional cotton/rayon menstrual products
rows.swap: Unscented organic-cotton products, or a medical-grade silicone cup
rows.note: Menstrual products contact absorptive tissue, and studies have detected fragrance chemicals and trace metals in some. Unscented, tested materials reduce that contact exposure.

rows.name: Baby Food Pouches (Heavy Metals)
rows.context: Commercial infant purees, especially rice-based ones
rows.swap: Vary grains away from rice and serve fresh homemade purees
rows.note: Investigations have found arsenic, lead and cadmium in some commercial baby foods, with rice-based products highest. Varying ingredients and making purees at home lowers the cumulative intake.

studies.claim: Among 564 US baby foods, including pouches, lead was detected in 37% and cadmium in 57%; products containing rice were higher in both, and organic certification made no difference.

rows.name: Laundry Detergent (1,4-Dioxane)
rows.context: Conventional and heavily fragranced laundry detergents
rows.swap: A fragrance-free detergent screened for 1,4-dioxane
rows.note: Some detergents contain 1,4-dioxane, a manufacturing by-product, plus fragrance allergens that linger on clothes against the skin. Certified fragrance-free products reduce both.

rows.name: Artificial Turf (Crumb Rubber)
rows.context: Synthetic sports and play surfaces with rubber infill
rows.swap: Natural grass where possible, and wash hands after play
rows.note: Crumb-rubber infill and turf fibres can contain PFAS, PAHs and metals. Skin and hand-to-mouth contact are the main routes, so washing up after use reduces it.

studies.claim: Total fluorine was found in all 51 artificial-turf samples from Stockholm, but extractable fluorine and targeted PFAS in under 42%; the authors attribute it to polymeric organofluorine that does not pose an imminent risk to users.

unsourced.reason: No study found that rates this mix of PFAS, PAHs and metals for players; the one turf PFAS study traced the fluorine mainly to polymers.
No study found that rates this mix of PFAS, PAHs and metals for players; the one turf PFAS study traced the fluorine mainly to polymers.

rows.name: Garden Hose Water
rows.context: Drinking from or filling bottles with a standard garden hose
rows.swap: A hose labelled drinking-water-safe (lead-free), and let it run first
rows.note: Ordinary hoses can leach lead, BPA and phthalates, especially after sitting in the sun. A drinking-water-rated hose and flushing the warm water first avoid most of it.

rows.name: Pressure-Treated Wood
rows.context: Chemically treated lumber for decks, raised beds and play sets
rows.swap: Seal it, or use untreated cedar or composite for garden and play surfaces
rows.note: Older pressure-treated wood used arsenic-based preservative; newer types use copper compounds that can still leach. Sealing the wood or choosing untreated material limits skin and soil contact.

rows.name: Aerosol Air Freshener Spray
rows.context: Spray-can room and fabric fresheners
rows.swap: Open a window, or simmer citrus peel and herbs
rows.note: Aerosol fresheners release VOCs and often phthalates as fragrance carriers, which you then inhale in an enclosed room. Ventilation addresses odour at the source rather than masking it.

studies.claim: Off-the-shelf UK domestic aerosol sprays were measured at source: household products such as air fresheners contained 62 wt% non-methane VOCs per can, and replacing LPG propellants with nitrogen showed a potential 50% emission reduction.

rows.name: Plastic Baby Bottles (Heated)
rows.context: Polypropylene bottles used for hot formula preparation
rows.swap: Glass or stainless-steel bottles, and cool water before it touches plastic
rows.note: Research published in Nature Food found polypropylene infant bottles release very large numbers of microplastic particles when formula is prepared at high temperature, with release rising sharply with water temperature. Preparing in a non-plastic vessel and cooling before transfer lowers release substantially.

rows.name: Paper & Bamboo Drinking Straws
rows.context: Plastic-free straws marketed as the eco option
rows.swap: Stainless-steel or glass straws, or simply no straw
rows.note: A Belgian survey published in Food Additives & Contaminants detected PFAS in the majority of paper and bamboo straws tested — often at higher rates than in plastic ones, because the coating that makes them water-resistant is itself fluorinated. Reusable metal or glass avoids the coating question entirely.

studies.claim: In 39 brands of straws sold in Belgium, PFAS were found in almost every material except stainless steel, and were detected more often in paper and bamboo straws.

Multiple studies link PFAS exposure to adverse immune outcomes in children, and dyslipidemia is the strongest metabolic outcome; cancer evidence is limited to manufacturing locations with extremely high exposures.

unsourced.reason: The straw study's abstract does not name which PFAS it found, and the human half-life studies found cover only long-chain PFAS, so none is cited.

rows.name: Unlined Copper Cookware
rows.context: Bare copper pots in contact with acidic food
rows.swap: Tin- or stainless-lined copper, or plain stainless steel
rows.note: Copper leaches readily into acidic foods, which is why food-safety codes restrict bare copper surfaces from contacting acidic ingredients. Lined copper keeps the heat-conduction benefit without the direct food contact.

rows.name: Imported Glazed Ceramic Dishware
rows.context: Traditional or artisanal glazed pottery used for food
rows.swap: Ceramics certified lead-free for food use, or plain porcelain and glass
rows.note: Health agencies have repeatedly documented lead leaching from traditional glazed pottery, particularly when it holds acidic or hot food. Decorative pieces are not always fired to food-safe standards; keep unverified glazed pottery ornamental.

rows.name: Decorated Vintage Glassware
rows.context: Enamelled or painted drinking glasses and dishes
rows.swap: Undecorated plain glass, or keep painted pieces for display only
rows.note: Analytical work published in Science of the Total Environment found lead and cadmium in the enamelled decoration on a large share of drinking glasses tested, including new items. The glass itself is inert — the concern is the exterior paint, especially where it meets the rim.

rows.name: Unvented Portable Kerosene Heater
rows.context: Flueless kerosene or paraffin space heaters
rows.swap: Vented heating, or electric heaters with a window cracked
rows.note: Any unvented combustion appliance puts its entire exhaust — nitrogen dioxide, carbon monoxide and fine particles — into the room it is heating. Vented or electric heating removes the combustion products from the indoor air entirely.

studies.claim: In a 27 m3 chamber study of unvented kerosene space heaters, both the semivolatile and the particle-bound organics they emitted were mutagenic in Salmonella typhimurium assays.

rows.name: 3D Printer Fumes
rows.context: Desktop filament printers running in an unventilated room
rows.swap: An enclosed printer vented outside, or a HEPA-and-carbon enclosure
rows.note: Melting filament emits ultrafine particles and VOCs, with emission rates varying widely by material — ABS is consistently measured higher than PLA. Enclosing and venting the printer, or running it in a room you are not sitting in, addresses most of it.

studies.claim: Five desktop 3D printers with up to nine filaments emitted ultrafine particles at median rates of about 10^8 to 10^11 per minute, plus VOCs such as styrene from ABS and HIPS (about 10-110 micrograms/min) and caprolactam from nylon-based filaments.

rows.name: Laser Printer Toner Emissions
rows.context: Office laser printers on or beside a desk
rows.swap: Site the printer away from desks in a ventilated space
rows.note: Work published in Environmental Science & Technology found some laser printers emit substantial ultrafine particles during printing, driven by the hot fuser. Distance and ventilation are the practical levers, since emission is highest right at the machine.

studies.claim: Of 62 printers in an office building, about 40% emitted submicrometer particles and 27% of those were high emitters; printer particles significantly affected submicrometer particle levels in the open-plan office (p = 0.01).

rows.name: Scented Wax Melts
rows.context: Flame-free warmers marketed as a cleaner alternative to candles
rows.swap: Unscented warmers, or ventilation instead of fragrance
rows.note: Because they are flameless, wax melts are often assumed to be the clean option. Research from Purdue published in Environmental Science & Technology Letters found they release high levels of fragrance terpenes that react with indoor ozone to form nanoparticles, at levels comparable to combustion sources.

rows.name: Ultrasonic Humidifier (Tap Water)
rows.context: Cool-mist humidifiers filled straight from the tap
rows.swap: Distilled or demineralised water, emptied and cleaned between uses
rows.note: Ultrasonic units aerosolise whatever is in the tank — dissolved minerals become the fine white dust that settles on surfaces, and a standing tank can grow microbial films. Distilled water and routine cleaning address both.

rows.name: Damp & Mould in the Home
rows.context: Persistent damp, condensation or visible mould growth
rows.swap: Fix the moisture source, ventilate, and keep humidity below 50%
rows.note: WHO guidance on indoor air quality treats persistent indoor damp as a well-established respiratory irritant. Remediation works on the water, not the mould — cleaning visible growth without fixing the moisture source simply lets it return.

rows.name: Nail Polish (Triphenyl Phosphate)
rows.context: Conventional polish containing TPHP as a plasticiser
rows.swap: Polish labelled TPHP-free, and apply in a ventilated room
rows.note: A study in Environment International measured a clear rise in a TPHP metabolite in urine after participants painted their nails, showing the plasticiser is absorbed rather than staying on the surface. TPHP-free formulations are now widely available and labelled.

rows.name: Keratin Hair Smoothing Treatments
rows.context: Salon smoothing systems that release formaldehyde when heated
rows.swap: Formaldehyde-free smoothing systems, or skip the treatment
rows.note: Occupational safety regulators issued hazard alerts after air testing found formaldehyde released during these treatments, including from products labelled formaldehyde-free. Salon workers carry the heaviest exposure because it is repeated daily.

rows.name: Gel Manicure UV Lamps
rows.context: UV curing lamps used to set gel polish
rows.swap: UV-protective fingerless gloves, or regular polish
rows.note: These lamps emit UVA. Laboratory work published in Nature Communications documented DNA damage in human cells exposed to gel-lamp radiation. Fingerless UV gloves are an inexpensive way to keep the exposure off the skin while still curing the polish.

rows.name: Recalled Hand Sanitiser (Benzene & Methanol)
rows.context: Gel sanitisers from unverified manufacturers
rows.swap: Soap and water where available; check recall lists for your brand
rows.note: Regulators issued extensive recalls after testing found methanol substituted for ethanol in some sanitisers, and independent laboratory testing later flagged benzene contamination in specific batches. Washing with soap and water avoids the supply-chain question altogether.

rows.name: Infant Rice Cereal (Inorganic Arsenic)
rows.context: Single-grain rice cereal as a first food
rows.swap: Rotate in oat, barley and multigrain cereals
rows.note: Rice takes up more inorganic arsenic from soil and water than other grains, and regulators set a specific action level for infant rice cereal because infants eat a large amount relative to body weight. Varying the grain is the straightforward move.

studies.claim: In a New Hampshire cohort of 759 infants, about 80% had rice cereal in their first year; at 12 months, infants who ate it had geometric mean urinary arsenic of 9.53 µg/L against 2.85 µg/L in those who ate no rice products.

EFSA's contaminants panel found chronic dietary inorganic arsenic linked to cancers of the skin, bladder and lung, treated it as a genotoxic carcinogen, and judged that adult exposure margins (2 to 0.4 for average consumers) raise a health concern.

rows.name: Ayurvedic Herbal Supplements
rows.context: Imported traditional herbal remedies
rows.swap: Third-party tested supplements carrying a USP or NSF mark
rows.note: Testing published in JAMA found detectable lead, mercury or arsenic in roughly one in five Ayurvedic products purchased in the United States, including products bought online. Independent third-party certification is the practical filter.

studies.claim: Of 193 Ayurvedic medicines bought online in 2005, 20.7% contained detectable lead, mercury or arsenic, with similar shares for US-made (21.7%) and Indian-made (19.5%) products.

rows.name: Herbal Teas (Pyrrolizidine Alkaloids)
rows.context: Botanical infusions drunk daily from one source
rows.swap: Rotate varieties and brands rather than drinking one blend daily
rows.note: European food-safety surveys have found pyrrolizidine alkaloids in herbal and tea products, arriving as weed contamination during harvest rather than from the named plant. Rotating what you drink keeps any single contaminated source from becoming a daily habit.

studies.claim: In 1,105 food samples from the European market in 2014-2015, 91% of (herbal) teas contained at least one pyrrolizidine alkaloid, at a mean of 460 µg/kg dry tea (6.13 µg/L as an infusion).

EFSA's contaminants panel set a reference point of 237 µg/kg body weight per day for the carcinogenic risk of pyrrolizidine alkaloids and concluded there is a possible concern for human health, in particular for frequent and high consumers of tea and herbal infusions.

rows.name: Hijiki Seaweed
rows.context: A specific sea vegetable used in Japanese cooking
rows.swap: Nori, wakame or kombu, which do not carry the same finding
rows.note: Food-safety agencies in several countries advise against eating hijiki specifically, after testing found inorganic arsenic at levels far above other edible seaweeds. This is unusual among sea vegetables — the common alternatives are not implicated.

studies.claim: Of 31 retail seaweed samples of five varieties, inorganic arsenic was found only in the nine hijiki samples, at 67-96 mg/kg; the other types were all below 0.3 mg/kg.

EFSA's contaminants panel found chronic dietary inorganic arsenic linked to cancers of the skin, bladder and lung, treated it as a genotoxic carcinogen, and judged that adult exposure margins (2 to 0.4 for average consumers) raise a health concern.

rows.name: Sea Salt (Microplastics)
rows.context: Salt evaporated from seawater
rows.swap: Mined rock salt, which does not pass through seawater
rows.note: Multiple international surveys have detected microplastic particles in the large majority of sea salt brands tested, tracking the plastic load of the source water. Rock salt comes from ancient deposits and consistently tests lower.

studies.claim: Across 39 salt brands, sea salts held 0-1,674 microplastic particles per kg (one outlier at 13,629), against 0-148 in rock salt; levels in unrefined sea salt tracked microplastic pollution in the surrounding seawater.

rows.name: Harvested Rainwater
rows.context: Roof-collected rainwater used for drinking
rows.swap: Drink mains water rather than untreated roof rainwater
rows.note: Rain carries PFAS: a 2022 global analysis in Environmental Science & Technology found PFOA and PFOS in rainwater often far above US EPA drinking-water advisory levels, and 28% of roof-harvested samples in an Arizona study exceeded the then 70 ng/L advisory. Roofs and tanks add their own: 1–4% of 100 Australian household tanks exceeded drinking-water health values for metals.

studies.claim: Multiple studies link PFAS exposure to adverse immune outcomes in children, and dyslipidemia is the strongest metabolic outcome; cancer evidence is limited to manufacturing locations with extremely high exposures.
In about 200 roof-harvested rainwater samples a year in Arizona (2017–2020), 28% exceeded the then US EPA advisory of 70 ng/L for PFOS plus PFOA, with a mean exceedance concentration of 189 ng/L.
Comparing global measurements with guideline levels, the authors conclude that PFOA and PFOS levels in rainwater often greatly exceed US EPA Lifetime Drinking Water Health Advisory levels.
Of 100 Adelaide household rainwater tanks, 1–4% exceeded Australian drinking-water health values for cadmium, iron, manganese, lead and arsenic; 67% of surveyed households drank the rainwater.

All PFAS contain perfluoroalkyl moieties extremely resistant to environmental and metabolic degradation; most are non-degradable or transform into stable PFAS products, so they classify as very persistent under EU chemicals rules.
After contaminated drinking water was replaced in Ronneby, Sweden, estimated mean serum half-lives were 5.3 years for PFHxS, 3.4 years for PFOS and 2.7 years for PFOA.

rows.name: Idling a Vehicle in an Attached Garage
rows.context: Warming up or running an engine with the garage door closed
rows.swap: Reverse out first, and never run an engine in a closed garage
rows.note: Exhaust in an attached garage carries carbon monoxide and benzene into the living space through the shared wall, and concentrations build quickly in an enclosed space. Backing out before starting removes the exposure completely and costs nothing.

rows.name: Conventional Blueberries
rows.context: Non-organic fresh or frozen blueberries
rows.swap: Organic blueberries, or a good rinse before eating
rows.note: EWG added blueberries to its Dirty Dozen after USDA testing found residues of organophosphate insecticides on a large share of samples. Organic removes the concern, and even conventional berries stay a nutritious choice once washed.

rows.name: Conventional Green Beans
rows.context: Non-organic fresh or frozen green beans
rows.swap: Organic green beans, or wash conventional ones well
rows.note: USDA sampling behind EWG's Dirty Dozen found residues of acephate — an insecticide the EPA banned on the crop decades ago — on some conventional green beans. Buying organic sidesteps it entirely.

rows.name: Conventional Bell Peppers
rows.context: Non-organic sweet bell peppers
rows.swap: Organic peppers, or wash and peel where practical
rows.note: Peppers sit high on EWG's Dirty Dozen because their thin skin retains multiple pesticide residues per sample. They are worth eating; buying the organic version is the clean upgrade.

rows.name: Conventional Celery
rows.context: Non-organic celery stalks
rows.swap: Organic celery
rows.note: Celery is a perennial Dirty Dozen entry: with no protective peel, USDA tests routinely find several pesticide residues on a single stalk. Organic is the straightforward swap.

rows.name: Conventional Cherries
rows.context: Non-organic fresh cherries
rows.swap: Organic cherries, or wash thoroughly
rows.note: Cherries appear on EWG's Dirty Dozen, with USDA testing detecting organophosphate residues on many samples. A thorough rinse helps; organic removes the issue.

rows.name: Conventional Potatoes
rows.context: Non-organic potatoes
rows.swap: Organic potatoes, or peel before cooking
rows.note: Conventional potatoes are treated with chlorpropham, a sprout-inhibitor found on the skin of many samples. Because potatoes are eaten so often, the cumulative exposure adds up — peeling or buying organic reduces it.

studies.claim: In stored potatoes treated with the sprout inhibitor chlorpropham, whole tubers carried about 15 mg/kg after 28 days and 9 mg/kg after 85 days, peels 20-50 mg/kg, and peeled tubers about 1 mg/kg.

rows.name: Skin-Lightening Creams (Mercury)
rows.context: Imported or unregulated skin-whitening and anti-aging creams
rows.swap: Avoid entirely; use mercury-free vitamin C or niacinamide brighteners
rows.note: The FDA and EPA warn that some imported skin-lightening creams contain mercury at dangerous levels, which absorbs through skin and accumulates in the body and nervous system. There is no safe use — check labels for 'mercurous chloride', 'calomel' or 'mercurio' and discard them.

rows.name: Kohl / Kajal Eyeliner (Lead)
rows.context: Traditional kohl, kajal, surma or tiro eye cosmetics
rows.swap: FDA-approved eyeliner from a regulated brand
rows.note: The FDA has repeatedly warned that traditional kohl and kajal can be largely lead salts, and their use near the eye is linked to raised blood-lead levels, especially in children. Only cosmetics with an FDA-approved colour additive list are safe substitutes.

rows.name: Imported Candy (Lead)
rows.context: Certain imported tamarind, chili or clay-based sweets
rows.swap: Reputable domestic brands; avoid candies in unlabeled or ceramic wrappers
rows.note: California and the FDA have documented lead in some imported candies, traced to chili powder, tamarind and the ink or ceramic of the wrapper. Children are most vulnerable; choosing regulated brands avoids the risk.

studies.claim: Oklahoma testing of two imported tamarind suckers found over half exceeded the FDA level of concern for lead; a child eating a quarter to a half of one a day would exceed the FDA's provisional tolerable intake, and the wrappers were high in lead.

rows.name: Vaping / E-Cigarette Aerosol
rows.context: Inhaling and exhaling e-cigarette vapour indoors
rows.swap: Quit vaping; seek nicotine-cessation support
rows.note: E-cigarette aerosol is not just water vapour: peer-reviewed analyses find heavy metals such as lead, nickel and chromium leached from the coil, plus formaldehyde and fine particulate. Secondhand vapour exposes bystanders too.

studies.claim: In six two-hour vaping sessions in a ventilated room, indoor air carried 1,2-propanediol, glycerine and nicotine, PM2.5 averaging 197 micrograms/m3, a 20% rise in PAH to 147 ng/m3 and a 2.4-fold rise in aluminium.

rows.name: Vinyl Tablecloth (Phthalates & Lead)
rows.context: Flexible PVC tablecloths and placemats
rows.swap: Cotton, linen, or PEVA/EVA tablecloths
rows.note: Independent testing has found flexible vinyl tablecloths that contain phthalate plasticizers and, in some products, lead used as a stabilizer — both of which can transfer to hands and food. Natural-fibre or PVC-free covers avoid it.

rows.name: Faux-Leather (PVC) Furniture
rows.context: Sofas and chairs upholstered in vinyl 'bonded leather'
rows.swap: Real leather, wool, or polyurethane (PU) upholstery
rows.note: Most inexpensive faux leather is PVC softened with phthalate plasticizers that migrate out and settle into house dust over the years you own the piece. Genuine leather, wool or PU alternatives skip the softeners.

rows.name: Costume Jewelry (Lead & Cadmium)
rows.context: Cheap metal fashion jewelry and children's trinkets
rows.swap: Solid stainless steel, titanium, or precious metals
rows.note: CPSC recalls and independent testing regularly find high levels of lead and cadmium in low-cost metal jewelry, a hazard mainly through skin contact and, for children, mouthing. Stainless steel, titanium or solid gold/silver are inert.

rows.name: Ceramic-Coated Nonstick Pans
rows.context: Sol-gel 'ceramic' nonstick cookware marketed as PFAS-free
rows.swap: Bare cast iron or stainless steel
rows.note: Ceramic nonstick avoids PTFE, which is a genuine plus, but the thin sol-gel coating wears off within a year or two and its full nanoparticle composition is rarely disclosed. Cast iron and stainless last for decades with nothing to shed.

unsourced.reason: No study measuring what sol-gel ceramic nonstick coatings release in use was found on PubMed.
No study measuring what sol-gel ceramic nonstick coatings release in use was found on PubMed.
No study measuring what sol-gel ceramic nonstick coatings release in use was found on PubMed.

rows.name: Bentonite Clay Detox Products (Lead)
rows.context: Edible 'detox' clay powders and cleanses
rows.swap: Skip clay cleanses; support your body's own clearance
rows.note: The FDA has warned that some edible bentonite clay 'detox' products contain elevated lead, which the clay draws from its geological source. Ironically, a product sold to remove toxins can add one — and there is no evidence it detoxes anything.

rows.name: Chewing Gum (Microplastics)
rows.context: Conventional gum made with a synthetic polymer base
rows.swap: Natural chicle-based gum, or skip gum
rows.note: The 'gum base' in most conventional chewing gum is synthetic rubber — essentially plastic. A 2025 laboratory study reported that chewing a single piece can release hundreds to thousands of microplastic particles into saliva. Natural chicle gum avoids the synthetic base.

rows.name: Conventional Pears
rows.context: Non-organic pears, eaten with the skin
rows.swap: Organic pears, or wash and peel conventional ones
rows.note: Pears appear on the EWG Dirty Dozen because residues of several pesticides are commonly detected. Washing helps and peeling removes more, though it also removes fiber.

rows.name: Conventional Nectarines
rows.context: Non-organic nectarines with edible skin
rows.swap: Organic nectarines, or thorough washing
rows.note: A recurring Dirty Dozen fruit: the thin, edible skin holds detectable multi-pesticide residues. Buying organic for the ones you eat most is a reasonable, budget-aware move.

rows.name: Canned Tomatoes (BPA-Lined)
rows.context: Acidic canned tomatoes in a can with epoxy lining
rows.swap: Tomatoes in glass jars or Tetra cartons, or fresh
rows.note: Acidity increases how much bisphenol migrates from an epoxy can lining into the food. Glass or carton packaging sidesteps the lining entirely.

studies.claim: EFSA's panel set a tolerable daily intake for BPA of 0.2 ng/kg body weight, with the immune system as the most sensitive target, and found average and high dietary exposures in all age groups exceeded it by two to three orders of magnitude.

rows.name: Swordfish (High Mercury)
rows.context: A large, long-lived predatory fish high on the food chain
rows.swap: Lower-mercury fish like salmon, sardines or trout
rows.note: Swordfish is on the FDA/EPA 'avoid' list for its high methylmercury content, which accumulates in the body. Pregnant people and young children are advised to skip it.

studies.claim: In muscle from 82 Pacific swordfish, total mercury ranged from 228 to 2,090 ppb; fish over about 96 kg dressed weight are predicted to exceed the 1,000 ppb action level used in the US, Canada and Europe.

In a Faroe Islands birth cohort of 1,022 children, prenatal methylmercury exposure from the mother's diet was linked at age 7 to poorer language, attention and memory, still seen after excluding children whose mothers had hair mercury above 10 µg/g.

In 27 volunteers who ate fish at the tolerable weekly methylmercury intake for 14 weeks, blood mercury rose from 6.7 to 26.9 ng/g, and its half-life after they stopped was 94 days (57 days after subtracting background).

rows.name: Rice-Based Drinks (Arsenic)
rows.context: Rice milk used as a dairy alternative
rows.swap: Oat, soy or pea-protein milk
rows.note: Rice concentrates inorganic arsenic from soil and water. UK and other agencies advise that young children in particular should not rely on rice drinks; other plant milks avoid the issue.

studies.claim: All 19 supermarket rice milks tested would fail the EU 10 µg/L drinking-water limit for arsenic, at up to 3 times that level; 80% of the 15 speciated samples had inorganic arsenic above 10 µg/L.

EFSA's contaminants panel found chronic dietary inorganic arsenic linked to cancers of the skin, bladder and lung, treated it as a genotoxic carcinogen, and judged that adult exposure margins (2 to 0.4 for average consumers) raise a health concern.

rows.name: Imported Farmed Shrimp
rows.context: Cheap imported farmed shrimp of uncertain provenance
rows.swap: Certified (ASC/BAP) or wild-caught shrimp
rows.note: Some imported farmed shrimp has been flagged for antibiotic and contaminant residues due to weak oversight. Certification schemes and known wild sources reduce that uncertainty.

studies.claim: Testing seafood bought in the US for 47 antibiotics, all 27 samples complied with FDA rules; residues were low, including sulfadimethoxine at 0.3 ng/g in farmed shrimp.

rows.name: Instant Noodle Cups (Boiling Water in Plastic)
rows.context: Pouring boiling water directly into a polystyrene or plastic-lined cup
rows.swap: Cook the noodles in a pot and eat from a ceramic bowl
rows.note: Boiling water in a plastic or foam cup increases microplastic and chemical migration into the broth. Transferring to a pot and bowl avoids heating the plastic.

rows.name: Lipstick (Lead & Metals)
rows.context: Colour lipstick reapplied throughout the day
rows.swap: Fewer reapplications and brands that publish metal-testing
rows.note: FDA surveys have detected trace lead and other metals in many lipsticks. Because lipstick is worn on the lips and partly ingested, frequency of reapplication is the main lever.

rows.name: Aerosol Hair Spray (VOCs)
rows.context: Propellant hair spray used in an unventilated bathroom
rows.swap: A non-aerosol pump spray, used with the door open
rows.note: Aerosols create a fine, easily inhaled mist of solvents and propellants. A pump product and good ventilation cut how much you breathe in.

rows.name: Petroleum-Based Lip Balm
rows.context: Mineral-oil / petrolatum lip balm applied and ingested daily
rows.swap: Beeswax or plant-oil balms from refined sources
rows.note: Poorly refined mineral oils can carry aromatic hydrocarbon impurities, and lip products are partly swallowed. Well-made plant- or beeswax-based balms avoid the concern.

rows.name: Scented Menstrual Pads
rows.context: Fragranced disposable pads worn against sensitive tissue
rows.swap: Fragrance-free or organic-cotton pads and tampons
rows.note: Added fragrance can include undisclosed phthalates and irritants placed against thin, absorptive skin. Fragrance-free products remove an exposure that serves no functional purpose.

rows.name: Octinoxate Sunscreen
